• heat gently / stop heating before all water has gone to avoid spitting
• use tongs to handle the hot dish
• keep hair tied back

parts.text: A student wants to find the solubility of a salt at 20 °C. Describe a method she could use.

rows.answer:
Any four from:
• add salt to a known mass/volume of water at 20 °C and stir until no more dissolves / some solid remains
• filter off the undissolved solid
• weigh an evaporating basin, add the saturated solution and weigh again
• evaporate to dryness and weigh the solid (heat to constant mass)
• solubility = mass of solid ÷ mass of water × 100

rows.answer: ethanol and water have boiling points that are close together

parts.text: Describe how a sample of pure water could be obtained from sea water in the laboratory.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 heat/boil the sea water (in a flask)
M2 water vapour/steam passes into a condenser
M3 vapour condenses and is collected (as distillate)

parts.text: Describe how a mixture of sand and salt could be separated to give a dry sample of sand.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 add water and stir (to dissolve the salt)
M3 wash the sand (residue) with water and leave to dry / dry in a warm oven

parts.text: Describe how crystals of copper(II) sulfate can be obtained from a solution of copper(II) sulfate.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 heat to evaporate some of the water (until crystals start to form / saturated)
M2 leave the solution to cool (and crystallise)
M3 filter off the crystals and dry them (between filter paper)

parts.text: Describe how crystals of potassium nitrate can be obtained from a solution of potassium nitrate.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 heat to evaporate some of the water (until crystals start to form / saturated)
M2 leave the solution to cool (and crystallise)
M3 filter off the crystals and dry them (between filter paper)

parts.text: Describe how crystals of zinc sulfate can be obtained from a solution of zinc sulfate.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 heat to evaporate some of the water (until crystals start to form / saturated)
M2 leave the solution to cool (and crystallise)
M3 filter off the crystals and dry them (between filter paper)

parts.text: Describe how fractional distillation separates a mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 heat the mixture
M2 ethanol vapour (lower boiling point) rises up the fractionating column
M3 water condenses in the column and drips back
M4 ethanol passes into the condenser and is collected (at 78 °C)

parts.text: Describe how you would carry out paper chromatography to find out how many dyes are in a black ink.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of the paper and put a spot of ink on it
M2 place the paper in a beaker of solvent with the solvent below the baseline
M3 allow the solvent to rise up the paper (then remove)
M4 count the number of spots formed

parts.text: Describe how you could test whether a sample of a white solid is pure.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 measure its melting point
M2 pure if it melts at a sharp/fixed temperature (that matches the data value)

parts.text: Describe what happens to the vapour in the condenser during simple distillation.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 vapour is cooled (by the cold water)
M2 vapour condenses / turns to liquid

parts.text: Describe how you would separate a mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 use a magnet
M2 iron is attracted / pulled out, sulfur is left

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain a dry sample of chalk (calcium carbonate) from a mixture of chalk and water.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 filter the mixture
M2 dry the residue (in a warm oven / leave to dry)

parts.text: Describe how a chromatogram of an unknown food colouring could be used to show it contains the dye E133.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 run a spot of E133 next to the unknown on the same paper
M2 a spot in the unknown at the same height / Rf as E133

parts.text: Describe one difference between how a pure substance and a mixture behave when heated until they boil.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 pure substance boils at a fixed temperature
M2 a mixture boils over a range of temperatures

parts.text: Describe how you could obtain pure, dry crystals of benzoic acid from a mixture of benzoic acid and sand. Benzoic acid dissolves well in hot water but only slightly in cold water.

rows.answer:
Description covering (one mark each)
M1 add hot water and stir (to dissolve the benzoic acid)
M2 filter (while hot) to remove the sand
M3 cool the filtrate so crystals form
M4 filter and dry the crystals

parts.text: Explain why the spots on a chromatogram must be placed above the level of the solvent.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 otherwise the dyes would dissolve in the solvent (in the beaker)
M2 and would not move up the paper / no separation

parts.text: Explain why the baseline on chromatography paper is drawn in pencil and not in ink.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 pencil/graphite is insoluble in the solvent / will not move
M2 ink would dissolve and separate (and confuse the result)

parts.text: Explain how paper chromatography separates the dyes in a mixture.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 dyes have different solubilities in the solvent / different attractions to the paper
M2 so they move up the paper different distances

parts.text: Explain why the water in a condenser enters at the bottom and leaves at the top.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 the condenser fills completely with cold water
M2 so cooling is more efficient

parts.text: Explain why a mixture of sand and water can be separated by filtration.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 sand is insoluble (in water)
M2 so it is trapped by the filter paper while water passes through

parts.text: Explain why a mixture of copper(II) oxide and copper(II) sulfate solution can be separated by filtration.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 copper(II) oxide is insoluble (in copper(II) sulfate solution)
M2 so it is trapped by the filter paper while copper(II) sulfate solution passes through

parts.text: Explain why a mixture of chalk and water can be separated by filtration.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 chalk is insoluble (in water)
M2 so it is trapped by the filter paper while water passes through

parts.text: Explain why simple distillation cannot be used to separate a mixture of two liquids whose boiling points are close together.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 both liquids evaporate / boil at about the same time
M2 so the distillate is still a mixture

parts.text: Explain why the fractionating column is packed with glass beads.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 increases the surface area for condensation
M2 so the liquids separate better / repeated evaporation and condensation

parts.text: A student says that a dye which gives a single spot with one solvent must be a pure substance. Explain why this may not be correct.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 two dyes could have the same Rf / move the same distance in that solvent
M2 (so) repeat with a different solvent (to check)

parts.text: Explain why a spot that stays on the baseline does not dissolve in the solvent and what this means for identifying it.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 the substance is insoluble in that solvent
M2 so a different solvent is needed to separate / identify it

parts.text: Explain why crystallisation is used instead of evaporating to dryness to obtain crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 evaporating to dryness would remove the water of crystallisation
M2 so only anhydrous (white) powder / no proper crystals would form

parts.text: Explain why the melting point of an impure solid is not a single temperature.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 impurities change / lower the melting point
M2 different substances melt at different temperatures so it melts over a range

parts.text: Explain why a lid is placed on the chromatography tank.

rows.answer:
Explanation linking (one mark each)
M1 keeps the air in the tank saturated with solvent vapour
M2 so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper (and rises evenly)

parts.text: State why a pencil, not a pen, is used to draw the baseline in a chromatography experiment.

rows.answer: M1 pencil (graphite) does not dissolve / move with the solvent

parts.text: Give two ways of making sure the results of a chromatography experiment are valid when comparing an unknown dye with known dyes.

rows.answer:
Any two from:
• use the same solvent
• use the same piece of paper / same baseline
• spots the same size
• same time / same temperature

parts.text: A student's spots smeared into long streaks up the paper. Suggest one cause and how to avoid it.

rows.answer: M1 spot too large / too concentrated / too much ink
M2 use a small spot (with a fine capillary tube) and let it dry

parts.text: Suggest why a lid is placed over the beaker during paper chromatography.

rows.answer: M1 to stop the solvent evaporating (so it rises evenly)

parts.text: State why the paper must be removed before the solvent reaches the top.

rows.answer: M1 so the solvent front can be marked / measured (to calculate Rf)

parts.text: Some food colourings do not move from the baseline with water as the solvent. Suggest what the student should do.

rows.answer: M1 use a different solvent (e.g. ethanol)

parts.text: Describe how to measure the distances needed to work out an Rf value.

rows.answer: M1 measure from the baseline to the centre of the spot
M2 measure from the baseline to the solvent front

parts.text: Give one safety precaution when using ethanol as a chromatography solvent.

rows.answer:
Any one from:
• keep away from flames (flammable)
• use in a well-ventilated room

parts.text: Explain why the dots of ink should be small and dried before the paper is put into the solvent.

rows.answer: M1 small spots give clear / separate spots
M2 drying stops the ink spreading / running

parts.text: In a distillation experiment, suggest why anti-bumping granules are added to the flask.

rows.answer: M1 to give smooth boiling / stop violent boiling

parts.text: In a distillation experiment, explain why the bulb of the thermometer is placed level with the side arm.

rows.answer: M1 measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser
M2 to show which substance is distilling / its boiling point

parts.text: A student uses filtration followed by evaporation to get salt from rock salt. Suggest why her mass of salt was lower than expected.

rows.answer:
All two points needed, one mark each
• not all the salt dissolved (not enough water / stirring)
• some salt left in the residue / solution spat out on heating / lost on transfer

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain salt from a mixture of salt and sand.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 add water and stir to dissolve the salt
M2 sand is insoluble
M3 filter the mixture
M4 sand stays on the filter paper as the residue; salt solution is the filtrate
M5 heat the filtrate to evaporate some water then leave to crystallise
M6 filter off and dry the salt crystals / evaporate to dryness
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain pure water and solid copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) sulfate solution.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 heat the solution in a flask (simple distillation)
M2 water boils / evaporates and the vapour passes into a condenser
M3 vapour condenses and pure water is collected
M4 copper(II) sulfate stays in the flask
M5 for crystals: stop heating when saturated and leave to cool / crystallise
M6 filter and dry the crystals
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 heat the mixture in a flask fitted with a fractionating column
M2 ethanol has the lower boiling point (78 °C)
M3 vapours rise; water (higher boiling point) condenses in the column and returns
M4 thermometer at the top reads 78 °C while ethanol distils
M5 ethanol vapour condenses in the condenser and is collected
M6 change the collecting flask when the temperature rises above 78 °C
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain the dyes in a green food colouring and identify them.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 pencil baseline; spot of the colouring and spots of known dyes
M2 stand the paper in solvent below the baseline
M3 lid on; allow solvent to rise most of the way
M4 remove and mark the solvent front; dry
M5 compare heights of spots / calculate Rf values
M6 dyes with the same Rf / height as known dyes are present
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain iron filings, salt and sand from a mixture of all three.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 use a magnet to remove the iron filings
M2 add water to the rest and stir to dissolve the salt
M3 filter: sand is the residue
M4 wash and dry the sand
M5 evaporate / crystallise the filtrate to get salt
M6 dry the salt crystals
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain pure, dry potassium nitrate crystals from a mixture of potassium nitrate and charcoal powder.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 add (warm) water and stir to dissolve potassium nitrate
M2 charcoal is insoluble
M3 filter to remove charcoal
M4 warm the filtrate to evaporate some water until saturated
M5 cool to crystallise (solubility falls on cooling)
M6 filter and dry the crystals between filter paper
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain hexane (boiling point 69 °C) and heptane (boiling point 98 °C) from a mixture of the two.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 fractional distillation
M2 heat the mixture gently in a flask with a fractionating column
M3 hexane vapour reaches the top first (lower boiling point)
M4 collect the distillate while the thermometer reads about 69 °C
M5 change the receiver when the temperature rises
M6 collect heptane at about 98 °C
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain a sample of pure water from muddy sea water.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 filter to remove the mud (insoluble)
M2 the filtrate still contains dissolved salts
M3 distil the filtrate: heat to boil the water
M4 steam passes into a condenser cooled by water
M5 condenses to pure water which is collected
M6 test purity: boils at exactly 100 °C

parts.text: Describe how you would obtain zinc sulfate crystals from a mixture of zinc sulfate solution and unreacted zinc powder.

M2 collect zinc sulfate solution as the filtrate
M3 heat the filtrate to evaporate some water
M4 until crystals appear on a cold glass rod / saturated
M5 leave to cool and crystallise
M6 filter off and dry the crystals

parts.text: State the measurements needed to find the empirical formula of a metal oxide by burning the metal.

M2 mass of crucible + metal before heating
M3 mass of crucible + oxide after heating (to constant mass)

M2 so the mass of water calculated is not too small

M2 add a little dilute sulfuric acid / sodium sulfate

parts.text: Draw a labelled diagram of the apparatus for electrolysing a solution and collecting the gases formed.

rows.answer: M1 beaker/cell containing electrolyte with two electrodes
M2 electrodes connected to a d.c. power supply
M3 inverted test tubes over each electrode

parts.text: Describe what happens when molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Include the products at each electrode, half-equations and how you could identify any gaseous products.

rows.answer:
any six from:
M1 electrolyte contains ions that move when molten
M2 positive ions move to the cathode; lead formed
M3 cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (reduction)
M4 negative ions move to the anode; bromine formed
M5 anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation)
M6 lead: molten grey metal at bottom
M7 bromine: orange/brown vapour
rows.notes: max 6; one mark for each distinct creditworthy point; credit any other valid chemistry relevant to the question; IGNORE repetition of the same point
